topic.angle: The summer the Thames smelled so bad Parliament had to act and what it led to

card.title: The summer London held its nose

body.claim: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames smelled so bad that curtains in Parliament were soaked in lime chloride to mask the odour.
body.why: London's old sewers emptied untreated waste straight into the river, and the hot weather made the smell far worse. The Great Stink pushed Parliament to back Joseph Bazalgette's plan of big interconnecting sewers, built from 1859 to 1875. They ended the cholera outbreaks and still work today.

claims.claim: Claim/probe 1: in 1858 curtains in Parliament were soaked in lime chloride to mask the smell
claims.quote: the curtains on the river side of the building were soaked in lime chloride to overcome the smell

claims.claim: Claim: hot summer of 1858, the Thames smelled so bad
claims.quote: the hot weather exacerbated the smell of untreated human waste and industrial effluent that was present on the banks of the River Thames

claims.claim: Why: old sewers emptied untreated waste straight into the river
claims.quote: an ageing and inadequate sewer system that emptied directly into the Thames

claims.claim: Why: the Great Stink pushed Parliament to back Bazalgette's interconnecting sewers
claims.quote: The authorities accepted a proposal from the civil engineer Joseph Bazalgette to move the effluent eastwards along a series of interconnecting sewers
started at the beginning of 1859 and lasted until 1875

claims.claim: Why: they ended the cholera outbreaks
claims.quote: Bazalgette's work ensured that sewage was no longer dumped onto the shores of the Thames and brought an end to the cholera outbreaks

claims.claim: Why: the system still works today
claims.quote: His sewer system operates into the 21st century

claims.claim: Probe 2: engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed the sewer system
claims.quote: a proposal from the civil engineer Joseph Bazalgette
